fact: Catherine Marie Kerkow was born on October 6, 1951, in the coastal town of Coos Bay, Oregon.
Kerkow was the oldest of four children.
Kerkow attended Marshfield High School in Coos Bay.
Kerkow was a gifted track star and was a classmate of the famous long-distance runner Steve Prefontaine.
A former teacher described Kerkow as "quiet and unobtrusive."
Others remembered Kerkow as an "all-American girl" who regularly attended church.
When Kerkow's father Bruce left the family, the trajectory of her life seemed to change.
By early 1972, not long after high school, Kerkow left Coos Bay behind and headed to San Diego.
In San Diego, Kerkow took a job at a massage parlor.
One day in January 1972, Kerkow received a knock on the door while she was taking a shower, quickly put on a robe, and answered the door.
The man at the door asked Kerkow if her roommate, Beth Newhouse, lived there.
Kerkow told the man that Beth was probably out shopping at the drugstore.
About twenty minutes later, Beth returned with the same man, who introduced himself as Roger Holder.
After the three of them shared a joint, Holder invited Kerkow to join him for breakfast a few days later.
During their first date, Kerkow and Holder realized they had met years earlier as children in Coos Bay.
Willie Roger Holder was born in 1949 in Jacksonville, Florida.
Holder's father was posted to Coos Head Naval Facility in 1959, and the family briefly lived in Coos Bay.
The Holders were one of the only Black families in the area and were subjected to severe hostility and racial discrimination, eventually forcing them to move.
Holder enlisted in the U.S. Army and was sent to Vietnam, where he encountered disciplinary issues and was eventually discharged.
By the spring of 1972, Holder had concocted a plan he called "Operation Sisyphus."
The plan was to hijack a plane, demand the release of activist Angela Davis, fly her to North Vietnam, then escape.
On the morning of June 2, 1972, Kerkow and Willie Roger Holder boarded Western Airlines Flight 701, scheduled to leave Los Angeles International Airport for Seattle with a stopover in San Francisco.
Flight 701 carried 97 passengers in addition to Kerkow and Holder.
Holder carried a black Samsonite briefcase onto the plane.

Holder placed two index cards on the galley counter for a flight attendant to read, then opened the briefcase to reveal an alarm clock wired to what looked like explosives, which were in reality fake components.
Holder told the flight attendants, "I don't want to hurt anyone. But this is a bomb. There's a concussion grenade in here and eight slabs of C-4."
Holder was escorted into the cockpit, where he met Captain Jerry Owen, First Officer Fred Jones, and Flight Engineer Gerry Tinker.
Holder introduced himself politely to the cockpit crew, even shaking the captain's hand.
Holder demanded the plane be diverted to San Francisco International Airport, $500,000 in cash delivered on the tarmac, and Angela Davis freed from jail and flown with them to Hanoi, North Vietnam.
When the plane landed in San Francisco, Western Airlines delivered $500,000 in cash and placed it on the steps of the jet.
In exchange for the money, the hijackers released half the passengers in San Francisco, then crossed the country and released the other half in New York, where the plane was refueled.
Holder and Kerkow ordered the plane to take off again with only the crew, the cash, and their false bomb, with the new destination being Algiers, Algeria.
By the time the African coast came into view, the hijacking had stretched nearly 24 hours.

After arriving in Algeria, officials detained the pair briefly, quarantined them, and secured the $500,000 ransom; the Algerian government returned $488,000 of the ransom to U.S. officials while granting the couple political asylum.
Kerkow and Holder were released to Black Panther representatives; the International Section of the Black Panther Party was headquartered in Algeria and led by Eldridge Cleaver.
In a phone interview with an Oregon newspaper, Holder confided that he and Kerkow feared they would be killed by "shadowy establishment forces" targeting the revolutionaries.
By January 25, 1975, Holder and Kerkow had quietly left Algeria and surfaced in Paris, France.
Kerkow and Holder tried to enter France using fake passports, adopting the names Leavy Forte and Janice Ann Forte.
French police arrested them almost immediately on charges of illegal entry.
In April 1975, French judges ruled that hijacking was a "political offense" and, under French law, political crimes weren't grounds for extradition.
Holder and Kerkow parted ways sometime in 1977 after she told him she was going to Switzerland to acquire fake documents, and after that he never saw her again.
Holder returned to the United States in 1986 and spent two years in prison; he died in 2012 at the age of 62.
A federal arrest warrant was issued by the Eastern District of New York on June 5, 1972, charging Kerkow with air piracy, and that warrant remains active.
The FBI speculated that Kerkow could be in Oregon, France, Switzerland, Algeria, Jordan, or Cuba.
In 2022, to mark the 50th anniversary of the hijacking, the FBI renewed its appeal on social media, posting Kerkow's wanted notice and asking the public for tips.
